name: PT Barito Pacific Tbk

frontmatter.title: Barito Pacific: a large premium over fundamental parts
frontmatter.summary: Barito Pacific is the Prajogo Pangestu group's apex holding company. Under the Director ruling the konglo siblings are carried at their fundamental value, so the discounted parts are Rp418 a share and twelve-month fundamental value is Rp487; the price is 2.95x that value. The konglo lens keeps part of the premium and sets a Rp1,111 target, a total return of -9.8%: HOLD.
thesis: An apex holding company over two konglo siblings — Chandra Asri Pacific in petrochemicals, refining and infrastructure, and Barito Renewables in geothermal — plus smaller unlisted interests [S8].

Per the Director ruling of 31 October 2026, both siblings are carried at their fundamental twelve-month value, not at their lens targets, so the parent's own konglo overlay is applied once after the SOTP [S15, S16].
The discounted parts are worth Rp418 a share after the 30% holdco discount; the Rp1,235 price is 2.95x that value — a large premium to what we underwrite [S8, S15, S16].

Carrying the siblings at their lens targets instead would more than double the parts value; the assumptions file records that premium-carried case beside the base so the size of the ruling's choice is visible [S15, S16].

FY2025 profit is a non-cash bargain-purchase gain, and the nine-month 2026 profit fall is measured against that gain-inflated base; EBITDA of US$1,405.0m shows the operating business is profitable even as the third-quarter margin stepped down [S8, S17, S19].
The konglo lens reads the price as 2.95x fundamental value, keeps part of that premium for a year and sets a Rp1,111 target — a -9.8% return, hence the HOLD rating [S10, S11].

catalysts.event: MSCI opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status; feedback runs to 30 April 2027 and the decision is due by 30 June 2027 [S10]
Barito Pacific announced a share buyback programme [S4]
OJK sanctions in the BREN IPO allocation case, including a fine on AH Ltd for concealed controller-related allocations [S20]

Group targets installed geothermal capacity above a gigawatt by year-end 2026 after the Darajat retrofit, with the Chlor-Alkali/EDC project at an advanced construction stage and commissioning in 2027 [S17]

First step of the raised free-float minimum, to twelve and a half per cent; BREN's free float sits below that line and must be raised, with the binding fifteen per cent step due 31 March 2028, a forced step at the marked geothermal leg [S11, S12, S20]

Final free-float step to fifteen per cent: BREN's current registry reading of twelve point five eight per cent against a 31 March 2026 tier basis of twelve point three per cent must reach the floor by this date [S11, S12]
MSCI decision on Standalone status for Indonesia [S10]

blocks.text: **What changed.** Barito Pacific published nine-month 2026 results on 30 October 2026: revenue of US$8,690.0m, a large increase on the prior-year period, EBITDA of US$1,405.0m and net profit after tax of US$616.0m, with parent net profit of US$229.0m against US$582.0m a year earlier on the same basis [S17, S18, S19]. The headline fall in profit is an acquisition-accounting effect, not a cash-earnings collapse: the prior-year comparative carries the one-off bargain-purchase gain booked on the Aster refinery acquisition [S8, F23], which completed in April 2025, and no gain comparable to it recurs in the current period, while EBITDA remains positive even as the third-quarter margin stepped down [S17]. Two bigger changes sit underneath. We carry the third-quarter step-down into the forecast — FY2026 blends the nine-month actual with a fourth quarter at the exit margin, and FY2027E onward is held at that exit margin [S17, S7]. And under the Director ruling of 31 October 2026 the konglo siblings are now carried at their fundamental twelve-month value rather than their lens targets, so the parts and the target are lower than in the prior version; the target is Rp1,111 and the rating is HOLD.

Barito Pacific is the apex holding company of the Prajogo Pangestu group. It controls two listed legs — Chandra Asri Pacific (TPIA), the petrochemicals, refining and infrastructure arm, and Barito Renewables (BREN), the geothermal generator — with smaller unlisted property and logistics interests around them [S8]. We stay at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp1,111 against a last price of Rp1,235, a total return of -9.8%.

The call turns on the marks, not on the operating cycle. After the 30% holdco discount the parts are worth Rp418 a share: that is the discounted fundamental value, not the gross asset value. At Rp1,235 the price is 2.95x the discounted value we underwrite, and still about twice the undiscounted parts — the undiscounted parts are the discounted figure divided by one less the 30% discount — so the shares trade at a premium at both levels, not at a discount [S8, S16]. The Director ruling of 31 October 2026 settles the sibling marks: TPIA and BREN are both konglo siblings, so each is carried at its fundamental twelve-month value from its house model [S15, S16], not at its lens target and not at market. The parent's own konglo lens is then applied once, after the sum-of-parts — the sibling premium is not counted twice.

The ruling is the swing factor, and the assumptions file records both sides of it. Carrying the siblings at their lens targets instead — the prior convention — would more than double the parts value and lift the target; the base does not do it, because a lens target embeds each sibling's own regime premium and that premium is a regime variable, not a fundamental input [S16]. BREN's target sits far above its fundamental, so the choice is material: at BREN's fundamental the geothermal leg contributes a minority of the parts rather than most of them, and the exact figures, with the premium-carried alternative, are recorded in the assumptions file.

The konglo lens then sets the twelve-month number. The price is 2.95x the discounted fundamental value — a large premium — and the lens keeps part of that gap for a year rather than closing it: fundamental twelve-month value is Rp487 and the target is Rp1,111 [S10, S11]. Even keeping part of the premium the target sits below today's price, because the premium is wide enough that partial compression outweighs the forward roll; the return is -9.8%, hence HOLD.

Three things move the value from here: the petrochemical and refining spread cycle at Chandra Asri, which the nine-month margin shows is already compressing; the MSCI and free-float calendar that sets the flow backdrop for concentrated-ownership names; and the path of BREN's own valuation work, which would replace the unpublished mark if it publishes [S8, S10, S11, S17].

Holding companies over listed subsidiaries are common on the Indonesia Stock Exchange: the family vehicle holds control stakes, the listed operating arms raise capital, and investors routinely compare the parent's market value with the value of its stakes. A gap between the two is normal rather than an anomaly, and its direction can be either a discount or a premium depending on flows and control.

Barito Pacific is a holding company. Its operating value sits in its subsidiaries rather than in a trading business of its own [S8]. The group is organised around two listed legs: petrochemicals and refining through Chandra Asri Pacific (TPIA), and geothermal energy through Barito Renewables (BREN), with property, logistics and other smaller interests around them [S8].

The petrochemical leg is the larger by revenue. Chandra Asri operates olefins, polyolefins, styrene monomer and butadiene production, and in 2025 it acquired an interest in a Singapore refinery, extending the group into refining and, subsequently, fuel retail [S8]. That acquisition is why group revenue and costs both step up sharply: the refinery is a high-throughput, low-margin business that changes the consolidated revenue base without lifting the margin proportionally [S8, S7]. Chandra Asri also owns sixty per cent of Chandra Daya Investasi (CDIA), the infrastructure arm that runs power, water, ports and storage for the same industrial estate, so the petrochemical leg carries an infrastructure business inside it rather than beside it [S8].

The energy leg is Barito Renewables, which the group controls through BREN and which operates Star Energy Geothermal's geothermal fields [S8]. BRPT's ownership of BREN is 66.7%, and its effective ownership of Chandra Asri Pacific is 38.5% [S8]. The geothermal portfolio reached 936 MW of installed capacity after the Darajat retrofit in October 2026, with a target above a gigawatt by the end of the year [S17].

The controlling shareholder is the Prajogo Pangestu family through the Barito group: the chairman's direct stake is 71.4% and the public holds 28.6% [S8]. The group's stated strategy is regional expansion of the petrochemical and energy businesses while maintaining sound governance at the portfolio-company level [S5].

The revenue and profit mix follows the same split. On a consolidated basis the petrochemical and refining leg dominates the top line, because a refinery processes large volumes at thin unit margins, while the geothermal leg contributes steadier, higher-margin revenue from contracted generation [S8]. Property, logistics and the remaining activities are small relative to the two legs and are not the swing factor in group earnings [S8].

Read as a portfolio rather than an operating company, the parent's job is capital allocation: choosing which leg to fund, when to bring in partners — as it did at Chandra Asri with Glencore and with the fuel-retail acquisition — and how much cash to upstream [S8]. That is why governance and group structure, not the parent's own trading, decide the value that reaches shareholders [S8].

The operating footprint is domestic at its base and increasingly regional at its edge: the petrochemical and geothermal assets are in Indonesia, while the refining and fuel-retail acquisitions extended the group into Singapore and the wider region [S8]. The parent's own head office functions — treasury, capital allocation and group governance — are the activities that sit directly at Barito Pacific rather than inside a leg, which is why the holdco-level cost base and debt are the bridge items between the sum of the parts and the value a parent shareholder captures [S8].

The petrochemical industry is cyclical and capital-intensive, and the group's position is that of a large domestic producer exposed to regional olefin and polymer spreads [S8]. The refining and retail assets acquired in Singapore broaden the group's footprint across Southeast Asia but tie it more tightly to refining margins and fuel-retail economics than to the polymer cycle alone [S8].
The geothermal business is a regulated, contracted, low-variable-cost generator — the more stable of the two legs, and the one the group added to balance the petrochemical cyclicality [S8].

The house macro deck reads the regime as cautious, with balance-of-payments pressure and Indonesian rate-sensitive domestic demand on avoid; for a dollar-indebted petrochemical group that argues against the premium the tape pays to our discounted house value [S21]. We translate the dollar accounts at the deck's spot rate of Rp18,138/USD rather than its FY2027E rate of Rp18,350/USD, so the rupiah target is stated on the spot cross; marking at the forecast would lift the rupiah value by the FX gap [S21, S0, S8].

Competitive positioning is best read through the group structure rather than at the parent: the parent's economics are the economics of its two listed legs. The barriers that matter are the scale of the petrochemical complex, its integration into refining, and the resource and licensing position of the geothermal fields [S8].

External influences are the petrochemical spread cycle, the rupiah and the regional refining margin environment, and — decisively for an apex holdco — Indonesian capital-markets policy toward concentrated-ownership names [S8]. The free-float rule now requires fifteen per cent with staged deadlines from 31 March 2027, and MSCI is consulting on moving Indonesia to Standalone status with a decision due by 30 June 2027 [S10, S11]. For a name whose marginal price is set by flows in a thin float, those rules matter more than the polymer spread over a twelve-month horizon.

Five forces, read at the group level: buyer power is moderate, since petrochemical products trade in liquid regional markets where no single customer sets the price, while geothermal output is sold under long-term contracts to a state utility, which concentrates buyer power there [S8]. Supplier power is meaningful because feedstock costs are set by global oil and gas prices the group cannot influence [S8]. The threat of substitutes is real in petrochemicals, where competing producers and recycled feedstock cap pricing power, and low in geothermal, where the resource is fixed [S8]. Rivalry is intense in petrochemicals and regional refining, where the group competes with larger integrated producers, and limited in geothermal, where licences and fields gate entry [S8]. Entry barriers are highest where capacity, integration and licences matter — the petrochemical complex and the geothermal resource — which is also where the group's moat sits [S8].

The group's market position is that of a large domestic champion in petrochemicals with a broadening regional refining and retail footprint, and a leading listed geothermal developer — a leader in its home market rather than a global price-setter [S8].

The regulation that matters most to the value of the parent is not industry regulation at all, it is capital-markets regulation. The exchange's treatment of concentrated-ownership names — the raised minimum free float with its staged deadlines and the removal of high-concentration names from the headline indices — together with the possibility of MSCI removing Indonesia from its emerging-market benchmarks, determines the flow backdrop against which this stock trades, and therefore how quickly any fundamental under-valuation or over-valuation is closed [S10, S11, S13]. Industry regulation, by contrast, is a second-order influence: petrochemical capacity, the CDIA infrastructure concessions and geothermal licensing shape the legs' own long-run economics but do not set the parent's discount or premium [S8].

Petrochemical producers convert oil- and gas-derived feedstock into olefins and polymers, and profitability hinges on the spread between feedstock and product prices rather than on volumes alone. Geothermal generators rely on long-term contracts and fixed resources, so their revenue is far less volatile than that of a chemical producer.

Group revenue stepped up sharply with the Chandra Asri refining acquisition: FY2025 revenue was US$7,630.7m, against US$2,387.0m in FY2024 [S8]. The step-up is an acquisition effect, not organic growth. The filed cost of revenues is 7,378 USD m and the filed gross profit is 253 USD m, which is what a reader sees first [S8]. The engine's cost-of-goods line is US$7,082.8m, because the filed figure already contains the depreciation that the same annual report reports separately at 309 USD m; the two presentations therefore produce the same EBIT of US$-204.8m and the same EBITDA of US$104.0m [S8].

That bridge matters for reading the trough. On the filed presentation the gross margin is a single-digit number, but it is after a depreciation charge that sits inside cost of revenues; on a cash-cost basis the margin is wider, and the segment note's result is 548 USD m [S8]. FY2025 EBITDA of US$104.0m is a genuine trough, but not because of a full year of the refinery: the Singapore refinery was consolidated from its 21 April 2025 completion, so FY2025 carried only a part-year and FY2026 is its first full year [S8]. The group's operating result barely cleared its depreciation, which is why the forecast is anchored on the H1-2026 actual rather than on this trough.

Reported profit is not a guide to that operating result. Profit for the year was 1,616 USD m and parent net profit was 489.8, but the statement includes a non-cash gain from a bargain purchase of 1,868 USD m [S8]. Strip the gain and the group is loss-making at the parent level: operating cash flow of 310 USD m is ahead of normalised earnings, so accruals are negative once the non-cash item is removed [S8]. We classify this as an optics-class effect to disclose, not a manipulation flag — the gain is disclosed, audited and non-cash — but it makes the reported P/E meaningless.

The nine-month 2026 profit decline is the same phenomenon in reverse and must not be read as a cash-earnings collapse. Group net profit after tax was US$616.0m [S17], and parent net profit was US$229.0m against US$582.0m in the prior-year period, parent against parent [S19]; the whole of the fall sits in the comparison, because the prior-year nine months include the US$1,868.0m bargain-purchase gain on the Aster acquisition while the current period has no such gain [S8, F23]. The cash test is the EBITDA line, which is positive at US$1,405.0m [S17], and the group's net debt to equity was 0.77x at the period end [S17]. We therefore treat the profit drop as an acquisition-accounting effect — optics-class and disclosed — rather than as evidence of deteriorating cash earnings. The nine-month release carries no cash-flow statement, so the accruals ratio cannot be recomputed for the period; we state that gap rather than fill it [S17].

The forecast is anchored on the nine-month actual, not on the FY2025 trough. Revenue for the nine months to September 2026 was US$8,690.0m, of which the petrochemical and refining segment contributed US$8,190.0m and the energy segment US$501.0m, with only a small residual in other activities [S17]. EBITDA was US$1,405.0m, but that average hides a step-down: the first half earned a materially higher margin than the nine-month figure, so the third quarter ran well below it [S17, S7]. With the H1-2026 operating-cost and depreciation ratios held at 6.9% and 3.9% of revenue [S7, F38-F40], the cash gross margin input is 18.1% for FY2026E — the nine-month actual blended with a fourth quarter held at the third-quarter exit margin — and 15.0% from FY2027E, the exit margin carried forward [S17, S7]. No archived source explains a fourth-quarter rebound, so the base holds the exit rate and the fourth quarter at it, giving FY2026 revenue of US$11,586.7m and EBITDA of US$1,753.6m [S17, S8].

Against that forecast the nine-month actual is on track rather than behind: US$8,690.0m of revenue and US$1,405.0m of EBITDA for three quarters against full-year revenue of US$11,586.7m and EBITDA of US$1,753.6m [S17]. The margin path is flat from FY2027E at 15.0% to FY2035E at 15.0% — flat at the exit rate, not at the nine-month average — and the bear scenario, not the base, carries any further spread compression [S17]. The FY2025-to-FY2026 step is the largest calibration item and reflects the acquisition's first full year, not an unsourced margin assumption.

Interest and minorities are why parent earnings stay thin even as EBITDA recovers. FY2025 interest on financial liabilities not classified as fair value through profit or loss was US$379.3m, the LK's finance-cost-note interest line before bank charges, lease interest and deferred-financing amortisation, which together take total finance costs higher [S8, F43]. The forecast carries US$634.7m on the enlarged debt stack, so parent net profit is US$198.9m on the recovered operating base [S8, S7]. That parent line is model-derived, not a forecast of the reported parent result: the engine applies the modelled finance charge, tax rate and minority take-up to the annualised operating base, whereas the banked nine months of US$229.0m [S19] carry a lower minority share than the model assumes for the full year; the gap is interest, tax and minority timing, it does not imply a fourth-quarter parent loss in the reported accounts, and it does not enter the sum-of-parts, which carries no earnings weight [S8, S17, S19]. The large minority share — US$1,125.8m of FY2025 net profit — absorbs most of the operating result before it reaches the parent [S8]. The forecast parent profit is therefore a fraction of group EBITDA, and FY2025 parent profit is a bargain-gain artefact; this is why the valuation does not capitalise earnings.

The balance sheet carries meaningful leverage at the consolidated level. Consolidated net debt was US$4,543.2m at the end of FY2025, and most of it sits inside the listed legs — TPIA's refinery and chemical facilities, and BREN's geothermal project debt [S7, S8]. That is why the valuation deducts only the parent's own debt, not the consolidated figure: the listed legs are marked at their equity values, which already carry their debt, so netting consolidated debt again at the holdco level would double-count it [S7, S8]. The parent-only deduction is built from the Company's own balance-sheet items in the H1-2026 LK: its shelf-registration bonds [F11-F16], its two bank term loans [F17, F18], and its nil short-term bank loan at the half-year date [S7]. Parent-only cash is not separately disclosed in either statement, so the deduction is stated as the Company's own gross interest-bearing debt rather than a derived net figure [S7, S8].

On cash flow, the pattern to watch is the gap between EBITDA and free cash flow, because a refining and petrochemical business consumes working capital as throughput rises [S8]. FY2025 free cash flow was US$-1,005.1m, weighed down by the acquisition, the working-capital build and capital expenditure of 915 USD m [S8]. The group's capital allocation has been expansionary, so capex and financing flows are large relative to the parent's own resources [S8].

This is a holding company over listed stakes, so the primary method is a sum-of-parts [S8]. The house holdco card governs: listed stakes are marked at house value, holdco debt is deducted, and the resulting discount is treated as the base rate rather than as the opportunity. We do not use an earnings multiple, because FY2025 parent profit exists only because of the bargain-purchase gain, so a multiple on it capitalises a one-off [S8, F23]. We do not use a book multiple either: the same gain inflated book value, and the pre-acquisition five-year average is not a post-acquisition benchmark [S8]. That leaves the sum-of-parts as the only honest method, carrying 100% of the weight. This is a single-method valuation and we state the limitation: the DCF shown below is a sanity cross-check with zero weight, not an independent value, and the earnings and book multiples are unusable on a bargain-gain-distorted denominator [S8].

The marks follow the Director ruling of 31 October 2026 [S16]. TPIA and BREN are both Barito-group konglo siblings, so each is carried at its fundamental twelve-month value from its house model [S15, S16] — neither at its lens target and neither at market, so no sibling regime premium enters the parent's fundamental value. The stakes themselves are from BRPT's annual report [S8, F9, F10]. CDIA is not a separate line because it sits inside TPIA's own valuation; marking CDIA again at BRPT level would double-count it [S15]. The parent deduction is built from the Company's own debt items in the H1-2026 LK [S7, F11-F18], as set out in the financial section, and is gross parent debt with no parent cash netted; the assumptions file records that no parent-only cash balance is disclosed in either statement and quantifies the per-share effect of netting any, so the deduction is a stated conservatism rather than a measured one [S7, S8]. The consolidated associates and joint ventures of US$760.7m on the interim balance sheet sit inside the operating legs whose equity marks we use; the residual unlisted property and logistics interests are immaterial — the property segment result was US$5.9m before unallocated costs, and the other residual lines round away at the group level [S7, S8].

| Part | Mark | | --- | --- | | Chandra Asri Pacific, BRPT's effective stake | fundamental twelve-month value in the TPIA house model, not its lens target [S15] | | Barito Renewables, BRPT's direct stake | fundamental twelve-month value in the BREN house model, not its lens target; provisional until BREN publishes [S16] | | Chandra Daya Investasi | inside TPIA's own valuation; not separately marked [S15] | | Holdco debt | parent-only gross debt of the Company, not consolidated [S7, F11-F18] |

The discounted fundamental value is Rp418 per share — the sum of the fundamental-marked parts after the 30% holdco discount, not before it. The undiscounted parts are that figure divided by one less the discount. At Rp1,235 the price is 2.95x the discounted value we underwrite and, on the same arithmetic, about twice the undiscounted parts — a premium at both levels, not a discount [S8, S7]. The 30% base rate is the house anchor for a family-controlled holdco.

The nine-month result does not change those marks. TPIA and BREN are carried at their fundamental twelve-month values, so the parent's consolidated reporting period feeds only the zero-weight DCF cross-check and the earnings lines, not the sum-of-parts [S15, S16, S17]. What would change the marks is a revision to either sibling's fundamental model, a published covered target for BREN, or a group corporate action at the parent — not the accounting presentation of a profit decline [S15, S16]. A covered target would change the lens reading, not the fundamental mark.

The engine converts the discounted parts value into a twelve-month target in two steps. First it rolls the blended value forward at the cost of equity: Rp418 becomes Rp487 [S7, S15, S16]. Because the sibling marks are themselves twelve-month fundamental values, that roll embeds a second year of return; on a no-roll convention the base fundamental is the parts value itself and the target is lower still, so the HOLD does not depend on the roll — the roll if anything flatters the target, and we disclose that rather than editing the engine.

The BREN mark deserves its own reading because it is the largest single part and neither a market price nor a lens target. At BREN's fundamental the geothermal leg contributes a minority of the parts; carrying it at its lens target instead would make it the majority and more than double the whole parts value, with the exact figures and both sides recorded in the assumptions file [S16]. The difference is BREN's regime premium, which is a regime variable rather than a geothermal cash-flow fact. The base case follows the ruling; if BREN publishes and its covered fundamental moves, the BRPT SOTP moves with it.

The other listed leg carries endorsed upside of its own outside the base. TPIA's published coverage is ADD, with a lens target above its fundamental; the base carries TPIA at its fundamental, and the premium-carried sensitivity in the assumptions file shows what its lens target would add. A ten per cent cut to TPIA's fundamental mark lowers the parts value by roughly the same proportion and the target by less, the lens absorbing part of it — a direct test of the petrochemical spread path the nine-month print showed compressing [S15]. The announced buyback is sized against the free float in the assumptions file: at about three per cent of the tradeable stock it is a dated flow support rather than a valuation driver [S4].

The cost of capital is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, with a levered beta of 1.84, giving a cost of equity of 17.3% and a WACC of 10.5% on equity and debt weights of 43% and 57% [S8].

The konglo lens then converts fundamental value into the twelve-month target. The lens reads the price as 2.95x the discounted fundamental value — a premium, not a discount — and, over three regime scenarios independent of our business scenarios, keeps part of that premium for twelve months, so that target = fundamental value x the probability-weighted share of the premium retained. Fundamental twelve-month value is Rp487; the base regime scenario closes 30.0% of the log gap; after probability-weighting the three regime scenarios the target is Rp1,111 [S10, S11]. Because none of the regime flags fires for BRPT itself — it is not on the HSC list [S13], its own free float of 27.0% clears the fifteen per cent minimum, and no enforcement action names the parent — the compression is moderate rather than forced; the group's BREN leg does carry an OJK offering-case sanction, which is a risk at the marked subsidiary rather than a direct flag on the parent [S20].

The sensitivity grid shocks the holding-company discount and the cost of equity and reports pre-lens values; it does not bracket the target because the lens adds most of the distance to the price [S8]. The marks themselves are the larger sensitivity. The base carries both siblings at their fundamental values; the assumptions file also runs the premium-carried case, in which both are marked at their lens targets instead — that case more than doubles the parts value and lifts the target, and the reader can see the size of the ruling's choice there rather than having it buried in the base [S16]. The base is the clean reading of the ruling, not a cautious forecast: it is the value before the sibling premium. A ten per cent cut to TPIA's fundamental lowers the target by less than the cut, because the lens absorbs part of it [S15].

The heaviest risk is regime, not operations. The 2026 environment moved against concentrated-ownership names: MSCI froze index increases for Indonesian securities, deleted several large names from its Global Standard index in May, and opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status with a decision due by 30 June 2027 [S10, S14]. Domestically, the exchange raised the minimum free float to fifteen per cent on staged deadlines from 31 March 2027 to 31 March 2028 [S11]. For a name whose marginal price is set by flows in a thinly traded float, these are the risks that dominate the twelve-month path [S10, S11, S14].

BRPT's own index exposure is the part the archived sources do not settle. The MSCI consultation does not name BRPT, and the konglo registry records no index deletion for the parent; the May deletions are Barito-group siblings — BREN and TPIA — not BRPT itself [S14]. The forced-selling exposure is therefore indirect — through the value of the sibling marks and the flow backdrop for the group — rather than a direct deletion of BRPT from an index. We state that gap rather than infer a membership the sources do not show; the place to confirm it is the index provider's constituent file.

The subsidiary-level facts are starker than the parent's own. The konglo registry records BREN's free float below the fifteen per cent floor — twelve point three per cent at its 31 March 2026 tier basis, against a current exchange-registry reading of twelve point five eight per cent — and the rule runs on a two-step path: twelve and a half per cent by 31 March 2027, then fifteen per cent by 31 March 2028, which is the binding deadline for BREN. A forced float step by placement or rights issue therefore sits inside two years at the leg that under the old convention would have been the majority of the parts [S11, S12]. The same regime surfaced at BREN through enforcement: OJK sanctioned the parties behind the BREN IPO on 16 October 2026, fining AH Ltd for taking large allocations under concealed, controller-related identities and noting that the concealment left BREN's shares concentrated and its market float limited [S20]. A forced float increase would compress BREN's premium rather than its fundamental, which is exactly why the base now carries the sibling at fundamental and takes the premium only through the parent's own lens; we treat the action as a premium catalyst, not a fundamental one [S16, S20].

Operationally, the petrochemical spread cycle and the integration of the acquired Singapore refinery are the swing factors; a spread reversal from the H1-2026 level is the operating risk, and it is carried in the bear case rather than in the base, which steps to the third-quarter exit margin from FY2027E [S8, S7, S17]. The reported profit line will keep falling year on year while the prior-year bargain-purchase gain remains in the comparative; that is an accounting optic, and we watch EBITDA and cash conversion instead of the headline [S8, S17].

Currency and leverage are secondary but real, given the debt taken on with the refinery. The parent's own debt is modest against the marked parts, but it is the Company's obligation and is deducted before the discount [S7].

Governance and structure risks — related-party transactions inside the group, cross-holdings, and the incentive to use the holding company for group corporate actions — are the discount's DNA and are discussed under governance [S8].

The konglo lens is where the twelve-month number comes from, and it must be read alongside these business scenarios. Today's price is 2.95x fundamental value — a premium, not a discount — so the lens works to keep part of that premium rather than to close a gap. Over the lens's three regime scenarios, independent of our business scenarios, the base regime scenario closes 30.0% of the log gap in twelve months, taking fundamental value of Rp487 to a base-regime target of Rp1,039; probability-weighting the three regime scenarios gives the Rp1,111 target [S10, S11]. The regime targets run from Rp674 in the case where the premium compresses fastest to Rp1,691 where it is retained most fully; the share kept is driven by the name's regime flags, none of which fires for this name as we read it, so the compression is moderate rather than forced [S10, S11, S13].

Business scenarios and regime scenarios are separate. Our business scenarios (bear/base/bull, base probability 50%) are mirrored around the base. In the SOTP that carries all the weight, the only moving part in a business scenario is the holding-company discount: the sibling marks are fixed by the Director ruling [S16], so the bear widens the discount and the bull narrows it. The revenue-growth and cash-gross-margin shocks move the DCF cross-check, which carries zero weight in the target; we keep them so the operating path is tested somewhere, but they are not what drives the scenario values [S8]. The pre-lens parts values run from Rp358 in the bear to Rp478 in the bull, against Rp418 in the base, and that spread comes from the discount alone [S8]. Regime catalysts carry dates: the MSCI standalone decision by 30 June 2027, the free-float path of March 2027 and March 2028, the periodic HSC reviews and the announced buyback [S10, S11, S13, S4].

Signposts that would change the view: a confirmed MSCI standalone decision, the staged free-float deadlines of March 2027 and March 2028, the HSC review cycle, a change in BREN's own coverage status that replaces the unpublished mark, material related-party or corporate actions at the group level, and the petrochemical spread path [S8, S10, S11, S13, S16].

Barito Pacific is a Prajogo Pangestu family-controlled holding company and the apex vehicle of the Barito group [S8]. The annual report shows the controller's direct stake at 71.4% and the public at 28.6% [S8]. The konglo lens uses the exchange registry free float of 27.0% [S12], a different measure from the annual-report public holding because it strips holdings the registry treats as non-free; it clears the fifteen per cent minimum that applies by March 2028 but is thin in absolute terms [S11]. The exchange's HSC list as of 22 October 2026 does not include BRPT, so it is not subject to the HSC index removals that hit several sibling names [S13], and its float clears the first deadline [S11].

At the subsidiary level the governance record is not clean, and that matters because BREN is a marked part. OJK sanctioned the parties behind the BREN IPO on 16 October 2026, including a fine on AH Ltd for concealed controller-related allocations, and said the concealment had concentrated BREN's ownership and limited its float [S20]. We treat this as a group-governance fact that supports the mid-range holdco discount rather than a finding against BRPT itself; it also argues against capitalising any sibling premium inside the parent's fundamental value, which is what the Director ruling requires [S16, S20].

The group structure matters for governance: the parent controls the listed legs, and value reaches parent shareholders as cash is upstreamed from them. Cross-holdings and asset transfers between siblings are the channel to watch, and the group's listed perimeter includes TPIA's sixty per cent ownership of CDIA, which keeps an infrastructure business inside the chemical leg [S8]. The dividend record supports the input rather than contradicting it: the Company paid no parent dividend in FY2025 and 5.0 USD m in FY2024, so we model a payout of 10.0% rather than the full distribution the earlier draft assumed; with parent earnings normalised negative, the forecast pays nothing [S8, F28].

The annual report carries an unqualified audit opinion, and the ownership section reviewed disclosed no pledge of the controller's BRPT shares [S8]. The Company's term loans are secured over shares in its petrochemical subsidiary, which is a structure to monitor rather than a finding [S7]. That is a checked absence in the sources reviewed, not proof that no pledge exists; the exchange shareholding filings are the place to confirm it.

Related-party gravity is quantified rather than asserted. Revenue from related parties was 195 USD m, or 2.6% of net revenue, in FY2025 [S8]. That is small as a share of the top line, so the discount here is not about the size of related-party sales; it is about structure — a controlling family, a thin float, shared service arrangements and the option value of group corporate actions. None of those is a finding of misconduct, but together they are why the holdco discount sits mid-range rather than at the low end [S8].

The konglo profile above is the engine's reading of the group, the controller, the free float against the regulatory floor, HSC status, index deletions and enforcement, with its sources. ESG exposures are concentrated in the petrochemical leg — emissions, process safety and feedstock transition risk — and in the geothermal leg's resource and land questions [S8].

Dated regime catalysts dominate the calendar: MSCI's standalone consultation and its June 2027 decision, the staged free-float path — twelve and a half per cent by 31 March 2027 and the binding fifteen per cent by 31 March 2028 — and the forced BREN float step it implies, the periodic HSC reviews [S13], the OJK offering-case sanctions at BREN [S20], and any group corporate action such as the announced buyback [S10, S11, S4]. On the operational side we monitor the petrochemical spread, refinery throughput and integration progress at Chandra Asri, and the geothermal resource position at Barito Renewables [S8]. Between updates the KPIs are the group EBITDA margin and its spread over the nine-month level, upstream dividend flows from the two listed legs, and any change to the controller's effective stake [S8, S17]. We also track the Chlor-Alkali/EDC project, at the company's stated construction stage and due to commission in 2027, and the geothermal capacity path past a gigawatt [S17].

We also track the structure of the float itself, since the marginal price of this name is set by flows rather than by fundamentals: the reported free float against the regulatory floor, the composition of the register between the controller and the public, and the liquidity of the shares [S8, S12, S11]. A move in any of these — a placement, a further buyback, an index event or a change in the controller's stake — is a signpost that can move the premium independently of the business [S4, S10]. The single largest analytical catalyst is BREN's publication: when BREN publishes, its covered target replaces the unpublished mark and the BRPT sum-of-parts moves with it [S16].

bear.narrative: Petrochemical spreads compress from the H1-2026 level and the Singapore refinery integration underdelivers, so the blended cash gross margin runs four points below the base and group EBITDA falls well short of the annualised run-rate; the konglo regime tightens (free-float step, MSCI standalone) and the holding-company discount widens from the base rate. In the SOTP only that discount moves the value; the operating shocks are carried by the DCF cross-check.

bull.narrative: Olefin and refinery spreads hold near the H1-2026 level and the acquired Aster assets lift throughput, so the blended cash gross margin runs four points above the base; index and free-float risk recedes and the holding-company discount narrows from the base rate. The discount, not the operating shocks, is what lifts the SOTP; the margin upside is tested in the DCF cross-check.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs holding-company discount and cost of equity

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026 is anchored on the nine-month actual, not on the FY2025 trough: revenue for the nine months to September 2026 was US$8.69bn, up 56.3% on the prior-year period, with the petrochemical and refining segment contributing US$8.19bn of it [S17, F45, F50]. The forecast annualises that nine-month run-rate (four-thirds of the period) because no archived source explains a fourth-quarter decline, so FY2026 carries the first full year of the acquired Aster refinery; from FY2027 growth steps down to high-single-digit, then toward nominal GDP and the 2% terminal rate, rather than extrapolating the acquisition step-up [S8]. The previous basis annualised H1-2026 revenue; the nine-month actual is the later and better anchor and lifts FY2026 revenue by about 1.9% [S17, S7].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The engine's gross margin is revenue less the cash cost of goods (the raw-materials, production and manufacturing note), before the depreciation carried inside the filed cost of revenues. The forecast carries the third-quarter step-down into the base. The nine months earned EBITDA of US$1,405m on US$8,690m of revenue, a 16.17% EBITDA margin [S17, F45, F49], but the first half earned about US$1,043m of EBITDA on US$5,686m of revenue (18.35%) [S7, F36, F37, F39, F40], so the third quarter earned about US$362m on about US$3,004m of revenue, a 12.0% margin — a clear step-down. With the H1-2026 operating-cost ratios held (selling and G&A at 3.01% of revenue [S7, F39, F40]), the third-quarter cash gross margin is 15.05%. FY2026 is a blend: the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter exit margin, which gives a 18.15% cash gross margin; FY2027E onward is held at the 15.05% exit margin rather than the nine-month average. The prior basis held the 9M cash gross margin of 19.18% flat, which annualised the average of a declining path; the later actual is the better anchor and the residual compression stays in the bear scenario. FY2025 is not used: the Aster refinery was consolidated from its 21 April 2025 completion, so FY2025 carried only a part-year [S8, p.19]. [S8, S7, S17]

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total operating costs including the depreciation line, anchored on the H1-2026 actual: depreciation and amortisation of US$223.156m, selling costs of US$41.588m and G&A of US$129.654m on US$5,685.931m of revenue, or 6.94% of revenue [S7, F36, F38, F39, F40]. The prior basis called this "near the FY2025 actual" but used the three-year average, which was wrong; the refinery adds throughput with little incremental overhead, so the H1 intensity is held flat rather than stepped back up [S8, S7]. The nine-month release gives no operating-cost split, so the H1 intensity is carried unchanged; the residual compression in the nine-month EBITDA margin is therefore assigned to the cash gross margin, the only line the disclosure lets us identify [S17].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: H1-2026 actual depreciation and amortisation of US$223.156m on US$5,685.931m of revenue, or 3.92% [S7, F36, F38], held flat. The engine average (FY2023-FY2025) was 4.31% but it mixes the pre-acquisition years with the enlarged asset base, so the latest actual is the better anchor.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital intensity held near the FY2025 actual, reflecting ongoing plant maintenance at Chandra Asri and field development at Barito Renewables [S8].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Parent-level payout, not the consolidated dividends line: the Company paid no dividend in FY2025 and US$5.0m in FY2024 against parent net profit of US$56.5m, so the record supports a low single-digit-to-ten per cent payout rather than the one hundred per cent previously assumed, which no year in the record supports [S8, F28].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for the reporting currency, applied to a group anchored on petrochemical and geothermal assets [S8].

assumptions.label: Holding-company discount to SOTP
assumptions.basis: House holdco base rate 20-40% for a family-controlled Indonesian holding company; anchored mid-range because Barito Pacific upstreams cash but carries wide related-party gravity and a thin 27% float in a regime that is penalising concentrated ownership [S8]

challenges.challenge: Rp931 is presented as the "fundamental" discounted parts value, but 63.1% of the gross parts (US$4,684.1m of US$7,421.5m; 68% of NAV) is BREN marked at its unpublished house target, which is ~2.2x BREN's own house fundamental (Rp1,139.04 vs Rp527.14 on the assumptions' own figures). That is a regime premium sitting inside the "fundamental", against VAL_KONGLO_REGIME §3 ("the premium is a regime variable, not a valuation input") and §4 (an uncovered konglo sibling should wait in draft). The prior C3 disposition relied on the Director ruling; this update still never states that Rp931 is premium-inclusive or shows BREN at its fundamental within the main SOTP.
challenges.answer: The base SOTP now carries BOTH konglo siblings at their fundamental twelve-month value (TPIA Rp1,346.88, BREN Rp235.52), so the parent lens is applied once. The older lens-target convention is kept only as a labelled premium-carried sensitivity, so Rp931 is no longer presented as the fundamental.

challenges.challenge: The bren_mark_sensitivity block the report directs readers to for "the exact figures" no longer reconciles to the current model and is internally impossible. Contribution target/fundamental = 5,675.46/1,155.83 = 4.91x, but the per-share ratio is 1,139.04/527.14 = 2.16x — same stake, same share count, same FX cannot give two ratios. The model's actual BREN row is US$4,684.14m, not 5,675.46m; and the block's "discounted SOTP" 1,139.04 / "fundamental" 1,331.15 / "target" 1,410.5 do not match the packet's 931.47 / 1,088.42 / 1,335.
challenges.answer: Regenerated from the current model: base parts Rp418.22, fundamental twelve-month value Rp486.78, target Rp1,110.53; premium-carried parts Rp931.47, fundamental Rp1,088.42, target Rp1,335. The impossible 4.91x block is deleted; BREN is 31.9% of gross parts at fundamental (63.1% in the premium-carried case), not four-fifths.

challenges.challenge: BREN's free float is 12.3% at 31 March 2026 (coverage/universe/konglo.yaml, BREN.ff_rule_basis), below the 15% floor that binds by 31 March 2027 — a forced float step (placement/rights issue) at the subsidiary that is 63% of BRPT's SOTP. The report surfaces only BRPT's own float (26.96%, compliant) and never names BREN's shortfall or its deadline, even though the base case assumes BREN's premium persists for twelve months. This is exactly the kind of registry fact VAL_KONGLO §3/§5 requires.
challenges.answer: Added BREN free float below the fifteen per cent floor (12.3% at 31 March 2026 per the konglo registry) and the 31 March 2027 deadline as a dated group catalyst in §5 and §7, with the mechanism: a forced float step compresses the BREN premium, not its fundamental, which is why the base marks the sibling at fundamental and takes the premium only through the parent lens.

challenges.challenge: The konglo registry records OJK enforcement dated 2026-10-16 against parties behind BREN (offering case; AH Ltd fined Rp500bn for concealed controller-related IPO allocations). BREN is the SOTP's largest component, yet §5/§6/§7 discuss no subsidiary-level enforcement and the report's own konglo profile reads "enforcement: none" for the group. Governance is the discount's DNA at BOTH levels (VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT §5; EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS §4), so this bears on the warranted discount and on BREN's premium.
challenges.answer: Named the OJK action on the parties behind the BREN IPO dated 16 October 2026 (AH Ltd fined for concealed controller-related allocations, which OJK said concentrated BREN and limited its float) with source S20 in §5, §6 and §7, and tied it to the warranted holdco discount and to the case against capitalising any sibling premium inside the fundamental.

challenges.challenge: The update lowers the cash gross margin to the 9M level (19.18%) yet holds that 16.17% EBITDA margin flat for ten years, while Q3 2026 earned only ~US$361m EBITDA on ~US$3,004m revenue (~12.0%) versus ~18.4% in H1 — a 6pp step-down in the latest quarter. FY2026 revenue 11,586.7m and EBITDA 1,873.3m annualise the average of a declining path. §3 even says the spread is "already compressing", and §5 still says the base "holds the H1 margin", contradicting §3.
challenges.answer: Carried the third-quarter step-down into the base: FY2026E blends the nine-month actual with a fourth quarter at the exit margin (18.15% cash gross) and FY2027E onward is held at the 15.05% exit margin; the residual compression stays in the bear. The stale holds-the-H1-margin sentence in §5 is fixed, and drift.gross_margin is justified in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: TPIA is 36.9% of the gross parts and is carried at its ADD house target, which pre-dates the 9M results; the petrochemical leg is exactly where the Q3 spread compression landed. The report tests only the BREN mark (C1/C2) and offers no TPIA contribution or sensitivity, so a TPIA target cut — the more direct consequence of the 9M print — is invisible.
challenges.answer: TPIA is now carried at its fundamental per the ruling; its contribution is US$2,475.15m (about two-thirds of gross parts) and the premium-carried and ten per cent cut sensitivities are recorded. TPIA coverage is dated 29 October 2026, one day before the BRPT 9M release, so the spread sensitivity is the explicit test rather than an assumption that its target already reflects the print.

challenges.challenge: holdco_net_debt is the parent's GROSS debt (US$546.463m) with no parent cash netted, although a holdco that receives upstream dividends and holds term loans almost certainly carries parent-level cash; assumptions' own parent_cash_sensitivity concedes ~Rp13/share per US$100m (Rp27/share at US$200m). MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE and VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT §1 both specify holdco NET debt. The report calls this "the most conservative reading available" but still deducts it before the discount.
challenges.answer: Parent-only cash is not disclosed in either statement; §4 now states that explicitly, labels the deduction as gross parent debt, and points to the per-share gross-vs-net sensitivity recorded in the assumptions file (about Rp13/share per US$100m after the discount). The deduction is kept because no parent cash can be sourced.

challenges.challenge: The Rp1trn buyback (S4) is sized at ~Rp10.7/share and dismissed as "an execution tool, not a valuation driver". Against a 26.96% free float it is ~3% of the tradeable stock — a material flow support for a name whose marginal price the report itself says is set by flows, and a dated catalyst under VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT §3.
challenges.answer: Resized the buyback against the free float: about 3.2% of the 26.96% tradeable stock (about 0.8% of market value) and treated as a dated flow catalyst for the premium the lens retains, not dismissed as marginal.

challenges.challenge: TPIA's endorsed ADD upside (its published house target sits above its own price) is inside 36.9% of the gross parts but is never quantified, so the valuation section frames the SOTP exclusively as BREN's premium risk and gives the reader no measure of the endorsed upside it also carries.
challenges.answer: Quantified TPIA: US$2,475.15m at fundamental, about two-thirds of gross parts, with its published ADD lens target (Rp1,489.55) shown in the premium-carried sensitivity rather than inside the fundamental, per the ruling.

challenges.challenge: §3 states "Group net profit after tax was US$616.0m and parent net profit US$229.0m, against US$582.0m in the prior-year period", but US$582.0m is the prior-year PARENT figure (F48, S19), while US$616.0m is the current GROUP-after-tax figure (F46, S17). The comparison mixes bases and overstates the apparent fall in the group line.
challenges.answer: Restated on a consistent basis: parent net profit US$229.0m against US$582.0m parent against parent (S19), with the current group-after-tax figure US$616.0m presented separately (S17); the mixed-basis comparison is deleted.

missing_bull_case.note: TPIA (36.9% of gross parts) carries endorsed ADD upside that is never quantified; the Rp1trn buyback (S4) is dismissed as marginal though it is ~3% of the 27% free float; no group corporate-action or upstream-dividend upside is argued, so the SOTP reads as all-BREN-risk with no endorsed positives.

missing_bear_case.note: BREN's 12.3% free float (fund record, asof 2026-03-31) against the 15% floor and 31 Mar 2027 deadline, the 2026-10-16 OJK offering-case fine on BREN parties (Rp500bn), and a TPIA spread-compression sensitivity are all absent, although BREN is 63% of gross parts and 68% of NAV.

assumption_realism.note: Base holds the 9M blended 16.17% EBITDA margin flat to FY2035 while Q3 2026 ran ~12.0% (EBITDA 361 on revenue 3,004) vs H1 ~18.4%, and §3 concedes spreads are already compressing; §5 still says the base "holds the H1 margin" — stale text and an unsourced optimism on a cyclical.

evidence_and_citations.note: The load-bearing bren_mark_sensitivity block is stale: contributions 5,675.5m/1,155.8m imply a 4.91x ratio against the 2.16x per-share ratio (1,139.04/527.14), and the model's BREN row is 4,684.1m; its "discounted SOTP" 1,139.04 and target 1,410.5 do not match the packet's 931.47 and 1,335. "About four-fifths of the gross parts" is actually 63%. The 9M source facts themselves check out.

valuation_method_fit.note: SOTP is the right primary method and CUAN/PTRO/CDIA are correctly excluded (CDIA inside TPIA; the others are not BRPT holdings). But Rp931 "fundamental" embeds BREN — an uncovered konglo sibling — at a house target 2.2x its own fundamental, i.e. a regime premium inside the fundamental (VAL_KONGLO §3/§4), and then BRPT's own lens keeps part of the price premium on top. Parent deduction is gross, not net debt.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is unusually candid — it states plainly the HOLD does not survive BREN at its fundamental. But "unchanged in substance" and "solidly positive" understate the Q3 margin step-down, and "about four-fifths" overstates BREN dependence at 63%; the tone leans on the marks while the operating data deteriorated.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck read correctly: spot FX Rp18,138 used in preference to the Rp18,350 forecast, 2% terminal growth, and the cautious regime with the MSCI/free-float calendar applied to §4/§5. The konglo deck drives the lens. Only gap is that the rate-sensitive/oil-import AVOID tags are not explicitly reconciled.

conservatism_audit.note: Parent-only GROSS debt of US$546.5m is deducted with no parent cash netted (Rp13-27/share, disclosed in parent_cash_sensitivity); the 30% holdco discount is mid-range against peer ABMM's 66.25%; payout held at 10% with zero DPS. Each is disclosed, but the bridge is one-sided and MOST_LIKELY calls for holdco net debt.

The 9M annualisation is the correct last-actual anchor under MOST_LIKELY. The residual issue is the flat-margin path, not the calibration gate itself.

findings.finding: The frontmatter summary reads "the discounted parts are Rp418 a share and twelve-month fundamental value is Rp487; the price is 2.95x that value". The 2.95x is price / discounted parts today (1,235 / 418.22); against the Rp487 twelve-month fundamental the same price is 2.54x (1,235 / 486.78). The body states the multiple correctly in both places, so the error is confined to the summary's antecedent.

Section 4 says a ten per cent cut to the TPIA mark lowers "the parts value by roughly the same proportion and the target by less". The recorded sensitivity runs the parts 418.22 to 384.71 (-8.0%) and the target 1,110.53 to 1,019.0 (-8.2%), so the target falls marginally more than the parts.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +13.8pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2026E is set on the nine-month 2026 actual, not a forecast drift: nine months to September 2026 earned EBITDA of US$1,405m on revenue of US$8.69bn, a 16.17% margin [S17, F45, F49], and the forecast annualises that run-rate with the H1-2026 cost and depreciation ratios held unchanged [S7, F38-F40]. No archived source shows a fourth-quarter decline [S17]. FY2025 is a part-year for the Aster refinery — consolidated from its 21 April 2025 completion — so its margin is not the anchor [S8, p.19]. The step is therefore the sourced nine-month actual, not an unsourced margin assumption.

Holding the 19.18% nine-month average flat would annualise the average of a declining path; the residual compression stays in the bear.
